warmup.q: A payment state machine is a switch over a sealed PaymentState with case branches for all five states and no default. You add a sixth record, Disputed, to the sealed interface. What happens when you build?
options: It compiles; Disputed payments go to the first matching case
It compiles; Disputed payments throw MatchException at runtime
It fails to compile at every switch over PaymentState that has no default
It fails only if a test calls the switch with a Disputed value
warmup.why: A switch expression over a sealed type must cover every permitted subtype, and with no default there is nothing to catch the new one, so javac reports "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" at each switch. That list of errors is exactly the list of places that need a rule. MatchException only appears when a subtype arrives from code compiled separately after the switch.

sections.h: State as data: a payment lifecycle in sealed types
sections.html:
A payment moves from Created to Authorized to Captured, maybe to Refunded, and can end in Failed. The GoF State pattern gives each state its own class with one method per event: CreatedState.capture() throws, AuthorizedState.capture() returns a CapturedState. That is five classes with four methods each, and the rules for one transition live wherever its class happens to be.

Java 21 and Kotlin let you write states and events as data and the rules as one function:

Java
sealed interface PaymentState permits Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Failed {}
record Created(String id) implements PaymentState {}
record Authorized(String id, String authCode, long amount) implements PaymentState {}
record Captured(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {}
record Refunded(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {}
record Failed(String id, String reason) implements PaymentState {}

sealed interface PaymentEvent permits Authorize, Capture, Refund, Decline {}
record Authorize(String authCode, long amount) implements PaymentEvent {}
record Capture() implements PaymentEvent {}
record Refund(long amount) implements PaymentEvent {}
record Decline(String reason) implements PaymentEvent {}

static PaymentState transition(PaymentState s, PaymentEvent e) {
    return switch (s) {                                  // no default: a new state breaks the build
        case Created c -> switch (e) {
            case Authorize(var code, var amt) when amt > 0 -> new Authorized(c.id(), code, amt);
            case Decline(var reason) -> new Failed(c.id(), reason);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);
        };
        case Authorized a -> switch (e) {
            case Capture() -> new Captured(a.id(), a.amount());
            case Decline(var reason) -> new Failed(a.id(), reason);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);
        };
        case Captured(var id, var amt) -> switch (e) {
            case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= amt -> new Refunded(id, r);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);
        };
        case Refunded r -> throw illegal(s, e);          // terminal
        case Failed f -> throw illegal(s, e);            // terminal
    };
}
Kotlin
sealed interface PaymentState {
    data class Created(val id: String) : PaymentState
    data class Authorized(val id: String, val authCode: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState
    data class Captured(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState
    data class Refunded(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState
    data class Failed(val id: String, val reason: String) : PaymentState
}
sealed interface PaymentEvent {
    data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentEvent
    data object Capture : PaymentEvent
    data class Refund(val amount: Long) : PaymentEvent
    data class Decline(val reason: String) : PaymentEvent
}

fun transition(s: PaymentState, e: PaymentEvent): PaymentState = when (s) {   // no else
    is PaymentState.Created -> when (e) {
        is PaymentEvent.Authorize if e.amount > 0 -> PaymentState.Authorized(s.id, e.authCode, e.amount)
        is PaymentEvent.Decline -> PaymentState.Failed(s.id, e.reason)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)
    }
    is PaymentState.Authorized -> when (e) {
        PaymentEvent.Capture -> PaymentState.Captured(s.id, s.amount)
        is PaymentEvent.Decline -> PaymentState.Failed(s.id, e.reason)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)
    }
    is PaymentState.Captured -> when (e) {
        is PaymentEvent.Refund if e.amount in 1..s.amount -> PaymentState.Refunded(s.id, e.amount)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)
    }
    is PaymentState.Refunded, is PaymentState.Failed -> throw illegal(s, e)    // terminal
}

Read it as a table. Each outer case is a state, each inner case is an event that state accepts, and everything else is illegal. Record patterns take fields out where you need them (Captured(var id, var amt)), and guards state what an event requires (when amt > 0). Kotlin's guards in when (is Refund if ...) became stable in Kotlin 2.2.0.

The function is pure: old state and event in, new state out, no I/O. You test it without mocks, and replaying history is one fold: val current: PaymentState = events.fold(Created(id), ::transition), which is how the lab's replay works. Keep side effects out of it. If capturing needs the PSP, call the PSP first and feed its answer in as an event.

try.title: Walk a payout through its states
steps: Open PayoutStateDemo.java (or .kt): a merchant payout with the same shape as the payment above. Predict the five lines.
Run it with the command below.
Change the approver from "dana" to " " (a blank name). Predict where the program stops and what it prints, then run.

code.title: PayoutStateDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.List; /** A merchant payout as a state machine: states and events are data, the rules are one pure function. */ public class PayoutStateDemo { sealed interface PayoutState permits Requested, Approved, Sent, Settled, Returned {} record Requested(String id, long amountMinor) implements PayoutState {} record Approved(String id, long amountMinor, String approver) implements PayoutState {} record Sent(String id, long amountMinor, String bankRef) implements PayoutState {} record Settled(String id, long amountMinor) implements PayoutState {} record Returned(String id, String reason) implements PayoutState {} sealed interface PayoutEvent permits Approve, Send, Confirm, BankReturn {} record Approve(String approver) implements PayoutEvent {} record Send(String bankRef) implements PayoutEvent {} record Confirm() implements PayoutEvent {} record BankReturn(String reason) implements PayoutEvent {} static PayoutState next(PayoutState s, PayoutEvent e) { return switch (s) { // no default: a new state breaks the build case Requested(var id, var amt) -> switch (e) { case Approve(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Approved(id, amt, who); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Approved(var id, var amt, var who) -> switch (e) { case Send(var ref) -> new Sent(id, amt, ref); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Sent(var id, var amt, var ref) -> switch (e) { case Confirm() -> new Settled(id, amt); case BankReturn(var reason) -> new Returned(id, reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Settled done -> throw illegal(s, e); // terminal case Returned done -> throw illegal(s, e); // terminal }; } // a second switch over the same states: the API's status label static String label(PayoutState s) { return switch (s) { case Requested r -> "pending approval"; case Approved a -> "approved by " + a.approver(); case Sent t -> "sent, bank ref " + t.bankRef(); case Settled d -> "settled"; case Returned r -> "returned: " + r.reason(); }; } static IllegalStateException illegal(PayoutState s, PayoutEvent e) { return new IllegalStateException(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " not allowed in " + s.getClass().getSimpleName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { PayoutState s = new Requested("po-31", 125_000); System.out.println(label(s)); for (PayoutEvent e : List.of(new Approve("dana"), new Send("DE-REF-0091"), new Confirm())) { s = next(s, e); System.out.println(label(s)); } try { next(new Requested("po-32", 900), new Send("DE-REF-0092")); } catch (IllegalStateException ex) { System.out.println("rejected: " + ex.getMessage()); } } }

try.expect: pending approval, approved by dana, sent, bank ref DE-REF-0091, settled, then rejected: Send not allowed in Requested. With a blank approver, the guard when !who.isBlank() fails, the event falls to the inner default, and the program stops at the first event with IllegalStateException: Approve not allowed in Requested. The guard is part of the rule, not a separate check.

sections.h: Let the compiler keep the to-do list
sections.html:
Chargebacks arrive, and a captured payment now needs a Disputed state. Add the record to the sealed interface and compile, before you write a single rule:

javac:   error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
kotlinc: error: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Disputed' branch or an 'else' branch.

Every switch over the state type fails, and each error points at one place: the transition function, the status label in the API, the metrics tag, the admin screen. The compiler has written your to-do list. Work through it, and the feature is done when the build is green.

That only works if you leave room for it. A default (or else) on a switch over your own sealed type means "and anything else", and the compiler believes you: Disputed falls into the default without a word. The inner switches in transition do use default, on purpose. Most (state, event) pairs are illegal, and listing each illegal pair adds nothing. So the rule is narrower than "never write default": never write it on the dimension you expect to grow. States grow. Here, the events within one state mostly don't.

The check happens at compile time, so there is a gap at run time, which Brian Goetz's design notes call the remainder: null, and subtypes added after the switch was compiled. A switch on a null state throws NullPointerException. If a new subtype arrives from a separately compiled jar, Java throws MatchException and Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for those cases, but a deploy that mixes old and new jars can hit them.

State and Strategy have the same structure: an object holds a value and behavior depends on it. The difference is who chooses. The caller picks a strategy, and it stays. A state machine picks its own next state as events arrive.

try.title: Add a state and read the errors
steps: In PayoutStateDemo.java, add record OnHold(String id, long amountMinor) implements PayoutState {} and add OnHold to the permits list. In Kotlin, add data class OnHold(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PayoutState inside the sealed interface.
Build it with the demo command. Before you look, predict how many errors you'll get and where.
Fix them: in next, an on-hold payout accepts nothing yet (throw illegal(s, e)); in label, return "on hold". Build again, then remove OnHold.

sections.h: Chain of Responsibility: pass it on, or answer now
sections.html:
A payment request passes logging, authentication, an idempotency check and fraud screening before any code charges the card. Each step may answer on its own (401, 409, "send to review") or pass the request on. That is Chain of Responsibility, and you use it every day. A servlet Filter gets the request and a FilterChain, and uses the chain "to invoke the next filter in the chain". OkHttp's Interceptor has one method, intercept(chain), and calls chain.proceed(request) to continue.

Each link is a function of the request and next, the rest of the chain:

Java
Interceptor auth = (r, next) -> r.headers().containsKey("Authorization")
        ? next.proceed(r)                              // pass it on
        : new Response(401, "no token");               // answer now: the rest never runs

Interceptor logging = (r, next) -> {
    Response res = next.proceed(r);                    // what follows runs on the way out
    log.info(r.path() + " -> " + res.status());
    return res;
};

Chain pipeline = chain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency, fraud), chargeHandler);
Kotlin
val auth = Interceptor { r, next ->
    if ("Authorization" in r.headers) next(r)          // pass it on
    else HttpResponse(401, "no token")                 // answer now: the rest never runs
}

val logging = Interceptor { r, next ->
    next(r).also { log.info("${r.path} -> ${it.status}") }   // runs on the way out
}

val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency, fraud), chargeHandler)

Code before next runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way out with the response, and not calling next at all is a short-circuit. Logging wraps everything; auth can stop a request before any later step sees it.

The GoF version links handler objects with setNext(). You don't need that. A list of functions and a fold make the chain, as the comparison below shows, and the result is immutable, so one pipeline serves every request on every thread. The lab's FraudChain.build copies the list it is given for the same reason: a later edit to the caller's list must not change a chain that is already in use.

try.title: Reorder two interceptors
steps: Read FilterChainDemo.java (or .kt). The third request has no token; the fourth is the client's fixed retry with the same idempotency key. Predict the four responses and the number of charges.
Run it with the command below.
Swap auth and idempotency in the list (List.of(logging, idempotency, auth)). Predict the last two responses and charges, then run.

code.title: FilterChainDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; /** An OkHttp-style interceptor chain in front of a charge endpoint. The order of the list is behavior. */ public class FilterChainDemo { record Request(String path, Map<String, String> headers) {} record Response(int status, String body) {} interface Chain { Response proceed(Request r); } interface Interceptor { Response intercept(Request r, Chain next); } // fold the interceptors into one chain, from the last to the first static Chain chain(List<Interceptor> interceptors, Chain terminal) { Chain next = terminal; for (int i = interceptors.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Interceptor ic = interceptors.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = r -> ic.intercept(r, rest); } return next; } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] charges = {0}; Set<String> seenKeys = new HashSet<>(); Interceptor logging = (r, next) -> { Response res = next.proceed(r); // in: nothing; out: log the status System.out.println(" log: " + r.path() + " -> " + res.status()); return res; }; Interceptor auth = (r, next) -> r.headers().containsKey("Authorization") ? next.proceed(r) : new Response(401, "no token"); // short-circuit: stop here Interceptor idempotency = (r, next) -> seenKeys.add(r.headers().get("Idempotency-Key")) ? next.proceed(r) : new Response(409, "duplicate"); Chain handler = r -> { charges[0]++; return new Response(200, "charged"); }; Chain pipeline = chain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency), handler); String token = "Bearer t0k"; System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7781")))); System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7781")))); System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Idempotency-Key", "order-7782")))); // token missing System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7782")))); // fixed and retried System.out.println("charges: " + charges[0]); } }

alt.title: FilterChainDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l09 // An OkHttp-style interceptor chain in front of a charge endpoint. The order of the list is behavior. data class HttpRequest(val path: String, val headers: Map<String, String>) data class HttpResponse(val status: Int, val body: String) fun interface Interceptor { fun intercept(r: HttpRequest, next: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): HttpResponse } // fold the interceptors into one function, from the last to the first fun chain(interceptors: List<Interceptor>, terminal: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse = interceptors.foldRight(terminal) { ic, next -> { r -> ic.intercept(r, next) } } fun main() { var charges = 0 val seenKeys = mutableSetOf<String?>() val logging = Interceptor { r, next -> next(r).also { println(" log: ${r.path} -> ${it.status}") } // in: nothing; out: log the status } val auth = Interceptor { r, next -> if ("Authorization" in r.headers) next(r) else HttpResponse(401, "no token") // short-circuit: stop here } val idempotency = Interceptor { r, next -> if (seenKeys.add(r.headers["Idempotency-Key"])) next(r) else HttpResponse(409, "duplicate") } val handler = { _: HttpRequest -> charges++; HttpResponse(200, "charged") } val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency), handler) val token = "Bearer t0k" println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7781")))) println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7781")))) println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Idempotency-Key" to "order-7782")))) // token missing println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7782")))) // fixed and retried println("charges: $charges") }

try.expect: In order: 200 charged, 409 duplicate (the same key again), 401 no token, 200 charged, and charges: 2; logging prints a line for every request, rejected ones included. After the swap, the 401 request records its key before auth rejects it, so the fixed retry gets 409 duplicate and charges: 1: the customer's payment never goes through.

sections.html:
Chains fail in four ways, and each looks like a bug somewhere else.

Order. Interceptors run in list order, and order is behavior. Put the idempotency check before auth, and a request rejected for a missing token has already used up its idempotency key, so the client's corrected retry gets 409 and the customer is never charged. Put logging after auth, and rejected requests never reach your logs. Pin the order with a test.

Forgetting next. A handler that returns without calling next and without a real answer drops the request silently. In a servlet filter, the client gets an empty 200. Every path through a handler must either call next or return a deliberate response.

Calling next twice. A retry wrapped around next.proceed(r) at the front of the chain repeats everything after it: the fraud check, the idempotency check and the charge. Put retries as close as possible to the call they retry, around the PSP client, not around the pipeline.

Exceptions. When a later handler throws, the code after next.proceed(r) in earlier handlers never runs. Timers, MDC cleanup and metrics belong in finally.

The same shape runs your Quarkus services. A CDI interceptor's @AroundInvoke method calls InvocationContext.proceed() to continue, and JAX-RS filters and CDI interceptors are ordered by @Priority. When a filter seems not to run, check its priority before you read its code.

analogy: A state machine is a board game's rule card: from this square, on this roll, you may move to that square, and nothing else. A chain of responsibility is the security line at an airport: ID check, bag scan, body scan, gate. Each station can wave you on or stop you, and the order matters, because there's no point scanning the bag of someone with no ticket. The analogy breaks on the way back. At an airport you never pass through security in reverse, but in a software chain the response travels back out through every station that let the request in, and each one can still change or log it.
world: Your payment and payout services already have state machines, often hidden in a status column and scattered if (status == ...) checks. Pull the rules into one pure transition function over sealed types, and the Oracle status column becomes a serialized state. A Temporal workflow is a durable state machine too: its history is the list of events, and replaying it rebuilds the state, which is why workflow code must be deterministic. On the chain side, Quarkus gives you JAX-RS ContainerRequestFilters and CDI interceptors ordered by @Priority, and Kafka clients take a list of ProducerInterceptors and ConsumerInterceptors in config order. In each, write down which link owns auth, idempotency and retries, and in what order they run.
mistake: The most common mistake is a default (or else) branch on the outer switch over your own sealed state type. It is often added "to be safe" or to silence a warning while the type is young. From then on, a new state compiles without a word and quietly takes whatever the default does, usually "reject every event", so disputed payments get stuck and nobody notices until support does. Leave the default off the switch over states, and let each new state break the build at every place that needs a rule. Use default only on dimensions you don't expect to grow, such as the illegal events inside one state, or on open sets you don't control, such as vendor codes.

compare.title: Building the chain: an index walker and a fold

java.title: RealChain.java
java.html: // OkHttp's shape: an immutable chain object that knows its position interface Chain { Response proceed(Request r); } interface Interceptor { Response intercept(Request r, Chain next); } record RealChain(List<Interceptor> interceptors, int index, Function<Request, Response> terminal) implements Chain { RealChain { interceptors = List.copyOf(interceptors); // cheap after the first time: copyOf keeps an unmodifiable list } public Response proceed(Request r) { if (index == interceptors.size()) return terminal.apply(r); // past the last link return interceptors.get(index).intercept(r, new RealChain(interceptors, index + 1, terminal)); } } Chain pipeline = new RealChain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency), 0, handler);

kotlin.title: Chain.kt
kotlin.html: // a function type replaces the Chain interface: the chain is just (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse fun interface Interceptor { fun intercept(r: HttpRequest, next: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): HttpResponse } fun chain(interceptors: List<Interceptor>, terminal: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse = interceptors.foldRight(terminal) { ic, next -> { r -> ic.intercept(r, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency), handler)

compare.note: Both call the interceptors in the same order and both are immutable. The Java record walks an index and creates a small chain object per step per request; that object is a natural place to carry more context, which is why OkHttp's real chain also exposes the call, its timeouts and the connection. The Kotlin fold builds the nested closures once, and next is a plain function, so no Chain interface is needed. Java can fold too, with a loop from the last interceptor to the first, as the lab's FraudChain.build does. What both languages make unnecessary is the GoF handler base class with a mutable setNext() link.

worked.title: Add chargebacks to the payment lifecycle

steps.say: A captured payment can now be disputed. A dispute ends either won (back to Captured) or lost (a new terminal state, ChargedBack). Start with data only: the new states and events.
steps.code: sealed interface PaymentState permits Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Failed, Disputed, ChargedBack {} record Disputed(String id, long amount, String caseId) implements PaymentState {} // 1. new states record ChargedBack(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {} sealed interface PaymentEvent permits Authorize, Capture, Refund, Decline, OpenDispute, WinDispute, LoseDispute {} record OpenDispute(String caseId) implements PaymentEvent {} // 2. new events record WinDispute() implements PaymentEvent {} record LoseDispute() implements PaymentEvent {}

alt.html: sealed interface PaymentState { // ...the five existing states, plus: data class Disputed(val id: String, val amount: Long, val caseId: String) : PaymentState // 1. new states data class ChargedBack(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState } sealed interface PaymentEvent { // ...the four existing events, plus: data class OpenDispute(val caseId: String) : PaymentEvent // 2. new events data object WinDispute : PaymentEvent data object LoseDispute : PaymentEvent }

steps.say: Compile before writing any rule. Every switch over PaymentState in the service fails. Count them: that is the size of the feature. Why do none of the inner event switches fail?
steps.code:
PaymentLifecycle.java:41: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
StatusLabels.java:12: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
LedgerMetrics.java:27: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

(kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is ChargedBack', 'is Disputed' branches or an 'else' branch.)

steps.say: The inner switches have a default, so the new events are simply illegal in the old states until you say otherwise. Now write the rules. Note the choice in step 5: no refund while a dispute is open, because the money may be going back through the card scheme already.
steps.code: case Captured(var id, var amt) -> switch (e) { case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= amt -> new Refunded(id, r); case OpenDispute(var caseId) -> new Disputed(id, amt, caseId); // 3. captured payments can be disputed default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Disputed(var id, var amt, var caseId) -> switch (e) { case WinDispute() -> new Captured(id, amt); // 4. won: back to captured case LoseDispute() -> new ChargedBack(id, amt); // 5. lost: terminal; no refunds meanwhile default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Refunded r -> throw illegal(s, e); case Failed f -> throw illegal(s, e); case ChargedBack cb -> throw illegal(s, e); // 6. terminal

alt.html: is PaymentState.Captured -> when (e) { is PaymentEvent.Refund if e.amount in 1..s.amount -> PaymentState.Refunded(s.id, e.amount) is PaymentEvent.OpenDispute -> PaymentState.Disputed(s.id, s.amount, e.caseId) // 3. captured payments can be disputed else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Disputed -> when (e) { PaymentEvent.WinDispute -> PaymentState.Captured(s.id, s.amount) // 4. won: back to captured PaymentEvent.LoseDispute -> PaymentState.ChargedBack(s.id, s.amount) // 5. lost: terminal; no refunds meanwhile else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Refunded, is PaymentState.Failed, is PaymentState.ChargedBack -> throw illegal(s, e) // 6. terminal

steps.say: Fix the label and metrics switches the same way, then pin the new paths in tests. Because transition is pure, a whole dispute is one replay call with no PSP and no database.
steps.code: @Test void lostDisputeEndsChargedBack() { var events = List.<PaymentEvent>of(new Authorize("A-77", 5_000), new Capture(), new OpenDispute("CB-310"), new LoseDispute()); assertThat(replay("p1", events)).isEqualTo(new ChargedBack("p1", 5_000)); } @Test void noRefundWhileDisputed() { assertThatThrownBy(() -> transition(new Disputed("p1", 5_000, "CB-310"), new Refund(100))) .hasMessage("Refund not allowed in Disputed"); }

alt.html: @Test fun `a lost dispute ends charged back`() { val events = listOf(PaymentEvent.Authorize("A-77", 5_000), PaymentEvent.Capture, PaymentEvent.OpenDispute("CB-310"), PaymentEvent.LoseDispute) val end: PaymentState = events.fold(PaymentState.Created("p1"), ::transition) assertThat(end).isEqualTo(PaymentState.ChargedBack("p1", 5_000)) } @Test fun `no refund while disputed`() { assertThatThrownBy { transition(PaymentState.Disputed("p1", 5_000, "CB-310"), PaymentEvent.Refund(100)) } .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException::class.java) }

lab.title: A payment state machine and a fraud-check chain
steps: Read the table in the Javadoc of PaymentLifecycle, and the given illegal and replay methods. Run the tests: all ten fail.
Write transition as a switch expression over the state with no default, and a switch over the event inside each state's case. Use record patterns and when guards for the amount rules.
In FraudChain, write build: copy the list, start from Chain next = terminal::apply, and loop from the last check to the first, wrapping next each time.
Write amountLimit and countryMismatch as one-line lambdas (r, next) -> ....
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then add a Disputed record to PaymentState (and to permits), build, read the error, and remove it.
hints: In a switch expression, case Refunded r -> throw illegal(s, e); is a complete case: a throw is allowed where a value is expected.
A lambda can only capture effectively final variables, so copy the loop variable first: Check check = copy.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = r -> check.check(r, rest);.
case Captured(var id, var captured) -> switch (e) { case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= captured -> ... } takes the fields out and states the refund rule in one line.

drill.title: Fold a chain from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write chain(interceptors, terminal) that folds a list of interceptors into one function, where each interceptor gets the request and next. Then answer: for [a, b, c], in what order do they run on the way in, and on the way out?

answer.html: static Chain chain(List<Interceptor> interceptors, Chain terminal) { Chain next = terminal; for (int i = interceptors.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { // wrap from the last to the first Interceptor ic = interceptors.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = r -> ic.intercept(r, rest); } return next; } // on the way in: a, b, c, then terminal; on the way out: c, b, a

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun chain(interceptors: List<Interceptor>, terminal: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse = interceptors.foldRight(terminal) { ic, next -> { r -> ic.intercept(r, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first // on the way in: a, b, c, then terminal; on the way out: c, b, a

recap: Model a lifecycle as sealed states, sealed events and one pure transition function. Record patterns and guards (when, or if in Kotlin 2.2+) state each rule in one line.
No default on the switch over states: a new state then fails to compile at every place that needs a rule. A default on the inner event switch is fine, because most pairs are illegal.
The compile-time check has a runtime remainder: null throws NullPointerException, and a separately compiled new subtype throws MatchException (Java) or NoWhenBranchMatchedException (Kotlin).
A pure transition function makes history a fold: replaying the events rebuilds the state, with no mocks needed in tests.
Chain of Responsibility: each link answers now or calls next. Code before next runs on the way in, code after it on the way out.
Chains break on order, a forgotten next, a doubled next and exceptions. Pin the order in a test, and put after-logic in finally.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why transition has no default on its outer switch but does have one on each inner switch, and what the compiler gives you when someone adds a Disputed state.
explain.answer: The outer switch is over states, and states are what we expect to add: disputes, holds, partial captures. With no default, the compiler knows the switch must cover every permitted state, so adding Disputed makes every switch over PaymentState in the code fail to compile. Those errors are the list of places that need a decision, and the feature is finished when the build is green. The inner switches are over the events one state accepts. Most events are illegal in most states, and new events usually only matter in one or two states, so a default that throws "not allowed" is the honest rule there. Putting a default on the outer switch would swallow the new state silently, and disputed payments would just reject every event at runtime.

deeper.html:
Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) and record patterns (JEP 440) both became final in JDK 21, so everything in this lesson compiles with --release 21 and no preview flags. In Kotlin, sealed subclasses must live in the same package and module as their parent, and guards in when with a subject became stable in 2.2.0.

Keeping the transition pure doesn't mean the machine does nothing. A common shape returns the next state together with a list of effects to run, such as "call the PSP", "post to the ledger" or "send a receipt", as sealed records. A thin outer layer executes them and feeds the results back in as events. Tests then assert on the returned effects, not on mocks. Temporal workflows work in a similar spirit: workflow code decides, activities do the I/O, and the history of events lets Temporal replay the workflow to rebuild its state.

Event sourcing takes replay to its end: store the events, not the state, and compute the state as a fold. Long histories get slow to replay, so systems store a snapshot every few hundred events and replay only what came after. That snapshot is a memento, from lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento.

Chain of Responsibility also shows up per method, not only per request. A CDI interceptor's @AroundInvoke method receives an InvocationContext and calls proceed() to continue to the next interceptor or the bean itself. Transactions, metrics and fault-tolerance annotations in Quarkus are built this way, which is why the proxy rules from Decorator and Proxy still apply to them.
